meta.title: Who really said "When the water reaches the upper deck, follow the rats"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mencken didn't coin it — he quoted it, as a familiar political maxim. It was in print by 1928, and quote dictionaries credit Claude Swanson instead.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the water reaches the upper deck, follow the rats'?
meta.ogDescription: Mencken quoted this line twice, both times as somebody else's saying. It was in print by 1928. Who coined it is undocumented.

answer.label: Not Mencken's own line — he was quoting a stock political maxim
answer.authorDates: In print by 1928 · quoted by H. L. Mencken in 1940 and 1941
answer.sourceLine: Mencken put the line in print twice — in his lecture “The Politician” (4 January 1940, collected in A Mencken Chrestomathy, 1949, p. 152) and in Newspaper Days, 1899–1906 (1941) — and both times he framed it as somebody else’s saying rather than his own. It was already in print in 1928, in Frank R. Kent’s Political Behavior, and no source we could verify records who said it first.
answer.confidenceText: Verified in Mencken's own books — as a line he was repeating, not coining.

source.excerpt: As we left him his interlocutor, a gentleman grown gray in Washington and long ago lost to every decency, pointed the moral of the episode… “When the water reaches the upper deck,” he said, “follow the rats.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its Misattributed section for Mencken, noting that he quotes it in Newspaper Days, 1899–1906 (1941) as a maxim he learned from Al Goodman.

The primary text bears that out. In the full scan of A Mencken Chrestomathy ↗, the line closes the essay “The Politician” on p. 152 — spoken not by Mencken but by “a gentleman grown gray in Washington,” a fellow reporter on a campaign train.

It was in circulation well before Mencken printed it: Internet Archive full-text search finds it in Frank R. Kent’s Political Behavior (1928) ↗ — “in other words he follows the rats when the water reaches the upper deck” — with no attribution at all.

Quotation dictionaries send the credit elsewhere entirely. A full-text sweep of scanned books ↗ turns up Hugh Rawson, A. K. Adams, William Safire and Bruce Bohle all filing it under Claude Swanson, several of them on the authority of the columnist Joseph Alsop.
source.excerptNote: From “The Politician” in A Mencken Chrestomathy, p. 152. The ellipsis omits a companion maxim the same speaker delivers first: “In politics,” he said, “man must learn to rise above principle.” Note who is speaking — not Mencken, but an unnamed veteran Washington reporter on a presidential campaign train.

source.rightsNote: The wording quoted here is Mencken’s transcription, and both books that carry it — Newspaper Days, 1899–1906 (1941) and A Mencken Chrestomathy (Knopf, published 10 June 1949) — were first published after 1930 and remain in copyright in the United States. The maxim as a spoken saying is older and unowned; Frank R. Kent’s 1928 Political Behavior, which prints a looser version of it, is itself in the public domain.

author.name: H. L. Mencken
author.heading: H. L. Mencken — the quoter, not the coiner
author.bio: Henry Louis Mencken was the most quotable American newspaperman of his century — a Baltimore Sun columnist, co-founder of The American Mercury, and author of The American Language, whose contempt for democratic pieties made him a permanent supplier of epigrams. That reputation is exactly why loose lines drift toward him: anything sour and well-turned sounds like something he would have said. In this case he did say it — out loud, in print, twice — but always with quotation marks around it and someone else’s voice inside them.

copyAttribution: "When the water reaches the upper deck, follow the rats." — an American political maxim of unknown authorship, in print unattributed by 1928 (Frank R. Kent, "Political Behavior"). H. L. Mencken quoted it, but did not coin it: in "The Politician" (A Mencken Chrestomathy, Knopf, 1949, p. 152) he gives it to an unnamed Washington reporter, and in "Newspaper Days, 1899–1906" (1941) he calls it one of "the familiar maxims of American statecraft." Quote dictionaries credit Claude Swanson, also without evidence. — quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them provable
misattribution.intro: This is a stock piece of American political cynicism that has been repeatedly adopted by whichever famous person happened to repeat it. Three claimants circulate, and the evidence for each is weaker than it looks.

items.why: Mencken printed it twice, which is how his name got attached — but in Newspaper Days he introduces it as one of “the familiar maxims of American statecraft” that he first heard from an older man, and in “The Politician” he gives it to an unnamed Washington reporter. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed to him ↗.

Hugh Rawson calls it “Swanson’s Law” and writes that Swanson “generally gets credit for devising this law, perhaps because he was secretary of the navy” — a hedge, not a citation. Swanson took over the Navy Department in 1933 ↗, years after the saying was already in print, and the reference books that credit him trace it no further back than a Joseph Alsop column.

In Newspaper Days Mencken says it was from this man that he “first heard all the familiar maxims of American statecraft.” Wikiquote names him as Al Goodman, and Carl Bode’s biography Mencken agrees — it was “from Al Goodman’s bearded lips” ↗ that Mencken first heard the companion maxim. Goodman passed the sayings on; nothing suggests he invented them.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who coined it. It was a piece of newspaper-and-lobby folklore before any of these three men repeated it — in print unattributed by 1928 ↗, and passed hand to hand from there.

context.heading: A maxim with two Menckens
lead: The line survives because it is a perfect joke about political survival: the rats are the professionals, and the professional’s skill is knowing exactly when to leave. Mencken loved it enough to use it twice, and using it twice is precisely what got his name welded to it.

But the two tellings do not match, and that is the tell. In Newspaper Days he files it among the stock sayings of the trade, picked up from an older Baltimore hand in his cub-reporter years. In “The Politician” — a lecture he gave at Columbia University on 4 January 1940 — it is the punchline of a campaign-train anecdote, delivered by a nameless correspondent “grown gray in Washington and long ago lost to every decency.” A man does not report his own epigram two different ways.
detailsBody: Frank R. Kent was a Baltimore Sun political columnist and a colleague of Mencken’s. His 1928 book Political Behavior — subtitled, aptly, The Heretofore Unwritten Laws, Customs and Principles of Politics as Practised in the United States — uses the saying in passing, folded into his own sentence and credited to no one: a politician, he writes, “follows the rats when the water reaches the upper deck.”

That is how genuinely proverbial sayings behave in print. They arrive already worn smooth, with no author attached, and only later acquire a famous owner. Mencken’s own description — “the familiar maxims of American statecraft” — says the same thing about where it came from: everywhere, and no one in particular.
